12. Need to accommodate all "gadgets"
Although several persons expressed the belief that by permitting ORV use on the public lands, "gadgeting" was being enhanced, we can find no merit in these statements. As a matter of fact, various kinds of ORVs are being used to a greater extent for commercial and official purposes on public lands because of their maneuverability and capacity for use in areas not otherwise accessible to ordinary type vehicles. Executive Order 11644 directed the Department of the Interior to manage and regulate ORV use of Interior lands so as to protect the resources of those lands, promote the safety of all users of those lands, and minimize conflicts among the various uses of those lands. Therefore, the Department recognizes the various types of ORVs and the many purposes for which they may be used under appropriate conditions, and has developed policies and regulations for managing the use of these vehicles on Interior lands in keeping with the intent of Executive Order 11644.
13. Economic impact and benefits from ORV use
There were eight incoming responses commenting on the draft ORV environmental statement which questioned inclusion of economic impacts in the statement. In summary: #19(a) Alaska Conservation Society - feels that discussion of economic impacts of ORV is useless, as well as fragmentary and undocumented; #26(b) Friends of Earth - feels economic impacts should be dropped from statement; #73(c) Idaho Environmental Council - feels economic boost is irrelevant and should not influence regulation of ORV; #74(d) Indiana Sassafras Audubon Society - feels economic boost is for temporary benefit of individuals and not for general public; #62(e) Natural Resources Defense Council - feels economic effects of ORV on rural economy and industry is not an environmental impact; #53(f) Desert Protective Council feels economic argument for ORVs out of place in environmental statement; #98(g) State of Colorado - questions economic benefits having direct correlation with ORV use; #94(h) Interior's Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife - recommended that economic benefits statement be eliminated; and #106(i) Interior's National Park Service suggested that for sake of balance, positive economic and social benefits, as well as negative effects should be identified and discussed in environmental statement.
The Department of the Interior believes that the environmental, social, and economic impacts of ORV use are all very closely interrelated and each warrants consideration in the environmental statement. The space available in this statement does not permit a full coverage of all aspects of economic impacts resulting from the sales of goods and services related to the use of all types of ORVs. However, data readily available to us indicate that the economic impact of the snowmobile industry and sport is very significant in some States. According to the April 1973 issue of Snowsports Dealer News, there are 19,582 people employed in Minnesota in either the manufacture or sale of snowmobiles, generating $126.7 million in taxable income for the State. Further, Minnesota's snowmobile manufacturers have a capital investment of over one quarter of a billion dollars. Also, the article reports that Minnesota receives an estimated $17 million per year in taxes, from personal, corporate, sales, and taxes from snowmobile gasoline and oil consumption.
